paperTitle: A Hybrid Rendering Approach for Fast and Realistic Reflections in Dynamic Scenes
centralContribution: This work presents a hybrid rendering approach for generating fast and realistic reflections in highly dynamic scenes with both rigid and deformable body simulations. It combines Screen Space Reflections (SSR) with a custom GPU ray tracing algorithm developed in CUDA, demonstrating improved efficiency and scalability compared to prior OptiX-based implementations, while achieving interactive frame rates and high visual fidelity, even with multiple reflection bounces.

units.title: Central Contribution
units.summary: Hybrid rendering for fast, realistic reflections in dynamic scenes.

content.description: The paper's core innovation is a hybrid rendering technique combining Screen Space Reflections (SSR) with a custom CUDA-based GPU ray tracer. This approach aims to achieve fast and realistic reflections in highly dynamic scenes involving both rigid and deformable body simulations, outperforming prior OptiX-based methods in efficiency and scalability, while maintaining interactive frame rates and high visual fidelity with multiple reflection bounces.

units.whyThisUnit: This unit highlights the main achievement and innovation of the research, serving as the core message of the exhibit.

units.title: Paper Abstract
units.summary: Summary of paper's context, problem, approach, and goals.

content.description: The paper addresses the computational challenge of achieving realistic real-time reflections in highly dynamic scenes. Traditional ray tracing is too costly, and existing hybrid methods or SSR have limitations like being restricted to static scenes, causing artifacts, or failing to integrate well with complex physics simulations, especially for deformable objects. The proposed solution integrates SSR with a custom CUDA GPU ray tracer and the Bullet Physics engine, employing a three-step process: initial SSR, followed by ray tracing for unsolved pixels (with multi-bounce support), and final image composition with Gaussian blur. A Linear Bounding Volume Hierarchy (LBVH) is used for efficient acceleration structure updates in dynamic scenes. This system aims for realistic reflections of various object types at interactive rates on accessible hardware.

units.whyThisUnit: Provides a comprehensive overview of the paper's motivation, methodology, and objectives, setting the stage for deeper exploration.

units.title: Hybrid Algorithm Workflow
units.summary: Visualizing the core hybrid reflection process.

content.description: This diagram illustrates the sequential workflow of the proposed hybrid reflection algorithm. It details how ray marching is initially used for screen space reflections, and if a reflection is not successfully generated for a pixel, ray tracing is then employed as an alternative to find the reflected surface for that specific pixel.

units.whyThisUnit: This figure is the central visual explanation of the paper's core methodology, making it a primary graphical representation.

content.caption: Fig. 2. Left: Reflections generated by our hybrid solution using ray tracing and SSR. Right: Reflections in Unreal Engine (version 4.17), using baked environmental maps and screen space reflections.

content.caption: Table 1: Rigid Body Simulation Performance (CUDA vs OptiX)
content.description: This table presents a comparative performance analysis of the CUDA and OptiX implementations for rigid body simulations. It shows execution times (ms) and frames per second (FPS) for varying numbers of Stanford Bunnies (5 to 30 objects), highlighting CUDA's superior efficiency.

content.caption: Table 2: Deformable Body Simulation Performance (CUDA vs OptiX)
content.description: This table details the performance comparison between the CUDA and OptiX implementations for deformable body simulations. It lists execution times (ms) and frames per second (FPS) across different counts of Utah Teapots (5 to 30 objects), affirming CUDA's better performance.
